title: Market Data: Feeds, ITCH/OUCH & FIX
tagline: How the market tells you what's happening — and the protocols an HFT system must parse at wire speed.

concept.analogy: Market data is the stadium's live scoreboard and play-by-play feed combined. A 'snapshot' is the full scoreboard right now (everyone's score). 'Incremental updates' are the play-by-play — 'team A scored 3', 'team B subbed a player' — tiny messages you apply to your own copy of the scoreboard. To stay in sync you number every play; if you miss play #58, you know to grab a fresh scoreboard before trusting your view again.
paragraphs: Market data is the stream of information exchanges publish about orders and trades. It comes in two complementary forms: snapshots (the complete current book state) and incremental updates (compact messages: order added/modified/deleted, trade executed). A consumer applies increments in sequence to a local book, using occasional snapshots to initialize or recover.

Protocols matter. Nasdaq's ITCH is a binary, order-by-order (L3) market-data feed — tiny fixed-layout messages designed for fast parsing. OUCH is its order-entry counterpart (you send orders). FIX is an older, text/tag-based protocol widely used for order entry and institutional connectivity — flexible but heavier to parse than binary feeds. Most exchanges also offer their own binary order-entry and data protocols.

Feeds are usually delivered over UDP multicast for low latency and one-to-many fan-out, often on two redundant lines (A and B) so a consumer can recover lost packets by arbitrating between them. UDP means no automatic retransmission — your handler must detect gaps via sequence numbers and recover, and must be robust to duplicates and reordering.

Parsing this at wire speed — tens of millions of messages per second — with zero allocation and minimal copying is a defining HFT engineering challenge, and a favorite interview/project topic (an ITCH parser).
points: Two forms: snapshots (full state) and incremental updates (add/modify/delete/trade).
ITCH = binary L3 market data; OUCH = order entry; FIX = tag-based, flexible, heavier.
Delivered over UDP multicast (low latency, fan-out), often on redundant A/B lines.
No retransmission on UDP — detect gaps by sequence number, recover via snapshot or the other line.
Goal: parse at wire speed with zero allocation and minimal copying.
concept.keyIdea: Market data is sequenced messages you apply to a local book. Binary L3 feeds (ITCH) over UDP multicast are parsed with zero-copy, gap-detecting handlers — the entrance to the whole trading pipeline.

deepDive.intro: From the wire to a usable book, here's the pipeline and the protocol realities.

steps.title: Depth levels: L1 / L2 / L3
steps.detail: L1 = top of book (best bid/ask + sizes). L2 = aggregated depth per price level (size at each price, not individual orders). L3 = order-by-order (every order with an ID), letting you track queue position. ITCH is L3. Richer depth = more data to process and more signal.

steps.title: Binary vs text protocols
steps.detail: Binary feeds (ITCH, exchange-native) use fixed or compact layouts you can often map directly onto a struct and read fields by offset — extremely fast. FIX is human-readable tag=value pairs delimited by SOH characters; flexible and ubiquitous for order entry, but parsing/serializing text is comparatively slow, so latency-critical paths prefer binary.

steps.title: Sequencing and gap recovery
steps.detail: Each message carries a sequence number. The handler tracks the expected next seq. A gap means lost packets: recover by reading the redundant line (A/B arbitration — take whichever line delivers first, fill gaps from the other), requesting a retransmission if available, or re-snapshotting. Until recovered, you should not trust the book.

steps.title: Zero-copy, allocation-free parsing
steps.detail: On the hot path you parse directly from the receive buffer (a view/span over the bytes) without copying into intermediate objects, and you reuse fixed buffers/object pools so there's no malloc per message. You decode just the fields you need. This is where C++ and careful memory layout pay off.

steps.title: Timestamps and time sync
steps.detail: Accurate, low-jitter timestamps (often hardware/NIC timestamps, with clocks disciplined by PTP) are essential to order events across feeds and to measure your own latency. We cover time sync in the networking lesson.

notes.title: The SIP vs direct feeds
notes.detail: In US equities, the consolidated SIP feed aggregates the NBBO across venues but is slower; HFT firms subscribe to direct exchange feeds and build their own consolidated view faster than the SIP. The latency difference between the SIP and direct feeds has itself been a competitive and regulatory topic.

pitfalls: Allocating per message (e.g., constructing objects/strings) — kills throughput; parse in place into reused structures.
Trusting the book through a sequence gap — detect and recover first.
Assuming UDP delivers in order and exactly once — handle reordering and duplicates.
Confusing ITCH (market data, inbound) with OUCH (order entry, outbound).

benchmark.intro: Rough throughput/latency intuition for parsing approaches (illustrative — exact numbers depend on hardware and message mix).

cells: Flexible, ubiquitous for order entry; too slow for the data hot path.
Better, but the copies and any allocation still cost.
Read fields by offset from the receive buffer; reuse buffers/pools. The HFT standard.

benchmark.takeaway: Binary, zero-copy, allocation-free parsing turns a per-message cost from microseconds into tens of nanoseconds — the difference between keeping up with the feed and falling behind it.

interviewQuestions.q: Why do feeds provide both snapshots and incremental updates? How do they work together?
a: Incremental updates are compact and let you keep a live book cheaply by applying small add/modify/delete/trade messages in sequence. But you need a starting point and a recovery mechanism — that's the snapshot, a full picture of the book at a known sequence number.

Workflow: on startup (or after a gap), take a snapshot at seq N, then apply increments N+1, N+2, … to keep the book current. If you detect a gap you can't fill from the redundant line, you re-snapshot to a new base and resume. Snapshots bound recovery cost; increments give low steady-state overhead.

interviewQuestions.q: Compare ITCH and FIX. Why might an HFT firm parse ITCH for data but tolerate FIX elsewhere?
a: ITCH is a compact binary, order-by-order market-data protocol with fixed message layouts you can read by offset with zero copy — built for speed and the high message rates of L3 data. FIX is a flexible, text-based tag=value protocol used widely for order entry and institutional connectivity; parsing/encoding text is slower and allocates more.

So firms use the fastest binary feed (ITCH or exchange-native) on the latency-critical data path, where every nanosecond and the message rate matter. FIX is acceptable on less latency-critical connections (e.g., some order entry, institutional links, or where a counterparty requires it) because its flexibility and ubiquity outweigh its speed cost there. Where order entry is latency-critical, firms use binary order-entry protocols (e.g., OUCH/native) instead.

interviewQuestions.q: Your UDP multicast handler sees sequence jump from 1041 to 1043. What happened and what do you do?
a: You missed message 1042 (a dropped/late UDP packet). UDP doesn't retransmit, so your local book may now be wrong.

Recovery: first try the redundant feed line (A/B arbitration) — the other multicast line likely delivered 1042, so you fill the gap from it. If that fails, use the venue's retransmission/recovery service if available, or re-snapshot to a fresh base sequence and resume applying increments. Critically, until you've recovered 1042 and re-synced, you treat the book as untrusted and stop quoting in that instrument to avoid acting on corrupt state.

interviewQuestions.q: What's the difference between L1, L2, and L3 market data, and when do you need each?
a: L1 (top-of-book): just the best bid/ask price and size (and last trade). Cheapest and smallest; enough for strategies that only care about the touch (simple taking, basic signals). L2 (depth-by-price / aggregated book): the total size at each price level on both sides — lets you see depth, compute imbalance across levels, and gauge liquidity. L3 (order-by-order / full book, e.g., ITCH): every individual order's add/modify/cancel with order ids, so you can reconstruct the exact queue and *your own queue position*.

You need L3 for queue-position-aware market making and the most precise microstructure signals (it's the most data and most processing). L2 suffices for depth/imbalance signals without per-order tracking. L1 is enough for coarse strategies and lowest cost/latency. More granularity means more bandwidth and more parsing work, so you consume the least data your strategy actually needs.

interviewQuestions.q: Why is exchange market data usually delivered over UDP multicast rather than TCP?
a: Because the exchange broadcasts the *same* data to thousands of subscribers simultaneously, and it needs minimum latency. UDP multicast lets the exchange send each packet once and have the network replicate it to all subscribers — efficient and fair (everyone gets it at nearly the same time). TCP is point-to-point and connection-oriented: per-subscriber state, acknowledgements, and retransmissions add latency, jitter, and don't scale to a one-to-many broadcast.

The trade-off is that UDP is unreliable (no retransmission, possible loss/reordering), so the exchange adds sequence numbers and provides redundant A/B feeds plus snapshot/retransmit channels, and each subscriber's feed handler must detect gaps and recover. This is the right design for low-latency fan-out: pay for reliability in the application layer (sequencing + recovery) rather than accept TCP's latency and scaling costs on the broadcast path.

Why send two identical feeds (A and B)?

problems.title: Sequence-gap detector
problems.statement: Implement a handler that processes messages tagged with monotonically increasing sequence numbers. It must: ignore duplicates/old messages (seq <= last applied), apply the next-in-line message (seq == last+1), and on a gap (seq > last+1) report the missing range [last+1, seq-1] and NOT apply the message (until recovery). Return the action taken for each incoming seq.
problems.hint: Track lastApplied. Three cases: seq <= lastApplied → 'duplicate'; seq == lastApplied+1 → 'apply' and advance; seq > lastApplied+1 → 'gap' covering lastApplied+1..seq-1.
problems.tests: Sequencing logic — the gate every feed handler needs.

approach: Keep a single integer lastApplied (start at the snapshot's base seq). For each message compare its seq to lastApplied+1.

If it's the expected next, apply and advance. If it's not greater than lastApplied, it's a duplicate/stale and is ignored. If it skips ahead, you have a gap of [lastApplied+1, seq-1]; report it and do not advance (real systems would now recover via the B-line or a snapshot before resuming).

problems.title: Detect and recover from a sequence gap
problems.statement: Your feed handler expects sequence 1001 next but receives 1005 on feed A. Moments later feed B delivers 1001, 1002, then jumps to 1006. Walk through how a correct handler classifies and handles these, what it does about the missing messages, and how it signals downstream consumers during recovery.
problems.hint: Track expected seq; ahead = gap (buffer/recover), arbitrate A/B by sequence taking the first copy, use snapshot/retransmit for true gaps, mark 'stale' until resynced.
problems.tests: Sequencing, A/B arbitration, and recovery logic.

approach: Expected = 1001. Feed A delivers 1005 — that's ahead of expected, so 1001–1004 are missing on A: a potential gap. The handler doesn't apply 1005 yet (applying out of order would corrupt the book); it buffers it pending the gap fill. Feed B then delivers 1001 and 1002 — these match/advance the expected sequence (arbitration: take the first feed to deliver each sequence), so apply them; expected becomes 1003. B then jumps to 1006, so 1003–1005 are now the outstanding gap (note A already has 1005 buffered, which fills part of it).

Recovery: the handler reconciles buffered messages across A and B by sequence — 1005 from A's buffer fills that slot; 1003 and 1004 are still missing from both feeds, a true gap. It requests a retransmission of 1003–1004 (if the exchange offers it) or re-syncs from the snapshot channel (which periodically broadcasts full book state), then replays buffered messages from the recovered point forward, returning to in-order processing. A/B arbitration means most one-feed gaps are instantly filled by the other feed, making true recovery rare.

Downstream signaling: while a genuine gap is unfilled, the book is not known-good, so the handler marks state 'stale' and the strategy stops quoting (or quotes conservatively) until re-synced — never trade on a desynchronized book. It also increments gap/recovery counters and alerts, so silent desync is impossible. Once 1003–1005 are recovered and applied in order, it clears 'stale' and resumes.

complexity.time: O(1) per message; recovery bounded by gap/snapshot size

problems.title: Estimate feed bandwidth and processing budget
problems.statement: A market-data feed averages 1 million messages/second, each ~50 bytes on the wire, but bursts to 5 million msgs/sec during the open. Estimate average and peak bandwidth, and the per-message CPU time budget you have if a single core must keep up at peak. What design choices follow from these numbers?
problems.hint: Bandwidth = rate × size. Per-message budget at peak = 1 second / peak rate. Compare to a cache-miss cost.
problems.tests: Sizing a feed handler from first principles.

approach: Average bandwidth ≈ 1e6 × 50 B = 50 MB/s (~400 Mbit/s). Peak ≈ 5e6 × 50 B = 250 MB/s (~2 Gbit/s) — so you need a 10GbE-class NIC and headroom. Per-message CPU budget at peak on one core = 1 s / 5e6 = 200 ns/message. That's only a few hundred CPU cycles — roughly the cost of a couple of cache misses.

Design implications: 200 ns/message rules out anything slow per message — no heap allocation, no locks, no syscalls, no fully decoding fields you don't need. You must parse zero-copy at fixed offsets with branch-light dispatch, keep hot state cache-resident, and batch-process bursts to amortize overhead and stay cache-hot. Receive rings and downstream queues must be sized for the 5×-burst (not the average) with back-pressure, or you'll drop messages and trigger expensive recovery. And because a single core is near its limit at peak, you pin/isolate that core and use kernel bypass so the OS doesn't steal cycles. The arithmetic directly justifies the whole low-latency feed-handler design.
